section_summary: This section comprises State Department records relating to Japanese internal economic affairs, corporate regulations, labor movements, and taxation from 1930 to 1939. It includes comprehensive embassy and consular despatches analyzing the factionalism and leadership of Japanese proletarian political parties, as well as the buyout of major foreign equity holdings in Nipponophone, Yokohama Rubber, and the Victor Talking Machine Company of Japan by domestic conglomerates like Nissan. Additionally, the records document diplomatic inquiries regarding Japanese wartime dividend limits under the National Mobilization Law and the application of the Business Profits Tax to American commercial purchasing operations.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference file note recording the attachment of a copy of Tokyo Despatch No. 24 regarding Japanese labor and proletarian parties.
subfiles.summary: Document file note referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 24 regarding the failure of Japanese laborers to support organized labor.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Tokyo Despatch No. 24

subfiles.about: A comprehensive report on Japanese proletarian political parties and labor unions prior to the 1930 general election.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Castle analyzes the disunity and factionalism among Japanese proletarian political parties and labor organizations ahead of the general election. He attributes the movement's weakness to personal rivalries among leaders, historical disputes over social theories, and widespread apathy among unorganized workers. He surveys the major proletarian parties—including the Social Democratic Party, Labor-Farmer Party, and Japan Popular Party—and encloses a chart illustrating their development.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 24: Developments in Japanese Proletarian Political Parties

subfiles.about: A document file note with an attached report extract regarding the introduction of the revised Labor Union Bill in the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Document file note and excerpt reporting that Home Minister Adachi introduced a revised Labor Union Bill favored by capitalists, sparking outrage among labor representatives.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and Extract on the Labor Union Bill

subfiles.about: Reports the sale of controlling interests in Nipponophone Company and Yokohama Rubber Company to Japanese corporate interests.
subfiles.summary: Consul Boyce reports that British Columbia and American Goodrich sold majority control in Nipponophone and Yokohama Rubber Company to Japanese investors, retaining royalties and technical advisors, as reported in The Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.title: Yokohama Despatch No. 129: Foreign Firms Surrender Control to Japanese Capital

subfiles.about: Reports the purchase of RCA's controlling interest in Victor Talking Machine Company of Japan by Japan Industry Company (Nippon Sangyo).
keywords: Victor Talking Machine Company of Japan
subfiles.summary: Consul Boyce reports that Yoshisuke Aikawa's Japan Industry Company (Nippon Sangyo/Nissan) acquired RCA's 68% controlling interest in Victor Talking Machine Company of Japan, giving Nissan 90% of the domestic phonograph market. RCA retains patent royalties, trademarks, and export protections, while Japanese military interest in RCA's television technology may have motivated the acquisition. Enclosures detail Nissan's extensive corporate holdings and review the history of Japan's phonograph industry.
subfiles.title: Yokohama Despatch No. 179: Victor Talking Machine Company of Japan Purchased by Japanese Capital

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for a report concerning the fiscal position of American companies in Japan in early 1939.
subfiles.summary: Document file note referencing a report on the fiscal position of American companies in Japan in early 1939.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Fiscal Position of American Companies in Japan

subfiles.about: Inquires about reported Japanese legislation limiting corporate dividend payments to shareholders.
subfiles.summary: Carrier Corporation inquires regarding reports of a Japanese law limiting corporate dividends payable to shareholders to ten percent of earnings.
subfiles.title: Letter from Carrier Corporation regarding Japanese Dividend Limitation Law

subfiles.about: Informs Carrier Corporation that its inquiry regarding Japanese corporate dividend limits has been referred to the Department of Commerce.
subfiles.summary: State Department informs Carrier Corporation that its inquiry into Japanese corporate dividend restrictions has been forwarded to the Department of Commerce.
subfiles.title: Letter to Carrier Corporation regarding Japanese Dividend Regulations

subfiles.about: Transmits an inquiry from Carrier Corporation concerning Japanese corporate dividend limitations for reply.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits Carrier Corporation's letter regarding Japanese dividend limitation regulations to the Secretary of Commerce for appropriate response.
subfiles.title: Letter to Secretary of Commerce Transmitting Carrier Corporation Inquiry

subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the State Department's letter regarding the referral of its dividend inquiry to the Department of Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Carrier Corporation acknowledges the State Department's letter and notes that it awaits communication from the Department of Commerce.
subfiles.title: Letter from Carrier Corporation Acknowledging Referral to Department of Commerce

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note and extract concerning the invocation of Article 11 of the National Mobilization Law restricting corporate dividends.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference note and report extract regarding Japanese government decree under Article 11 of the National Mobilization Law limiting corporate dividend increases.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note and Extract on Article 11 of National Mobilization Law

subfiles.about: Internal routing slip referring Scott, MacLeish & Falk's inquiry on Japanese business taxes to the Division of Foreign Service Administration.
subfiles.summary: Division of Far Eastern Affairs refers Scott, MacLeish & Falk's letter concerning Japanese business taxes on Butler Brothers to Foreign Service Administration.
subfiles.title: Department of State Routing Slip regarding Butler Brothers Tax Inquiry

subfiles.about: Inquires about a Japanese business tax assessed against Butler Brothers' buying office in Nagoya, Japan.
subfiles.summary: Scott, MacLeish & Falk requests State Department assistance regarding a Japanese business tax levied on Butler Brothers, arguing their Nagoya buying agency generates only purchasing expenses rather than taxable profits, and asks for legal recommendations.
subfiles.title: Letter from Scott, MacLeish & Falk regarding Japanese Business Tax on Butler Brothers

subfiles.about: Informs counsel that the inquiry regarding Butler Brothers' Japanese business tax has been forwarded to the American Vice Consul at Nagoya.
subfiles.summary: State Department acknowledges Leland K. Neeves's inquiry and notes that instructions have been transmitted to the Vice Consul at Nagoya.
subfiles.title: Letter to Leland K. Neeves regarding Japanese Business Tax Inquiry

subfiles.about: Instructs the Vice Consul at Nagoya to investigate the business tax levied on Butler Brothers and recommend suitable legal counsel.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Phillips instructs Vice Consul Stephan to investigate business taxes claimed from Butler Brothers and recommend suitable counsel.
subfiles.title: Instruction to American Vice Consul at Nagoya regarding Butler Brothers Tax Matter

subfiles.about: Acknowledges State Department's letter stating that the Butler Brothers inquiry was referred to the Vice Consul at Nagoya.
subfiles.summary: Leland K. Neeves thanks the Department of State for referring the Butler Brothers tax matter to the Vice Consul at Nagoya.
subfiles.title: Letter from Leland K. Neeves Acknowledging Action on Business Tax Inquiry

subfiles.about: Reports on the investigation into the Japanese Business Profits Tax assessed in connection with Butler Brothers' buying agency in Nagoya.
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul Stephan reports that Butler Brothers is not liable for the Japanese Business Profits Tax because it operates purely as a purchasing office with no local profits, whereas its buying agent Komaki Shokai is taxable on commissions and bonuses received. A conference between a visiting Butler Brothers representative, Mr. Komaki, and the consulate established that the apparent profit was merely an unspent expense allowance. Pertinent excerpts of the Business Profits Tax Law from the 1934 Japan Year Book are appended.
subfiles.title: Nagoya Despatch No. 36: Business Profits Tax on Komaki Shokai, Buyers for Butler Brothers, Chicago

subfiles.about: Transmits a copy of Vice Consul Stephan's despatch concerning the Japanese business tax matter to counsel for Butler Brothers.
subfiles.summary: Department of State transmits to Leland K. Neeves a copy of Vice Consul Stephan's despatch concerning Butler Brothers' tax liability.
subfiles.title: Letter to Leland K. Neeves Transmitting Report on Japanese Business Tax

subfiles.about: Expresses appreciation for the consular report clarifying Butler Brothers' business tax status in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Leland K. Neeves expresses appreciation to the State Department, noting that the Vice Consul's report greatly clarified Butler Brothers' situation.
subfiles.title: Letter from Leland K. Neeves Expressing Appreciation for Tax Clarification
